## Abstract

Emission reductions required to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement have been extensively 45

analyzed using integrated assessment modeling scenarios. However, the contribution of urban areas in aggregate, globally, by region and by city type, remains underexplored. Here, we develop a spatially explicit framework to downscale global emissions pathways to urban areas, differentiated by region and city type. Ambitious climate change mitigation could deliver 21 GtCO₂e of greenhouse gas (GHG) emission reductions in urban areas by 2050 relative to a 50

continuation of current policies and trends, primarily by transitioning away from fossil fuels in electricity and heat supply, deep decarbonization of industry, and mitigation in the transport and buildings sectors. Mitigation potential is concentrated in established and rapidly growing cities, reflecting their high current per-capita emission levels. Asian regions with high urbanization levels dominate global urban emissions and reduction potentials. The findings underscore the central 55

role of cities in achieving global climate targets and highlight the importance of differentiated mitigation strategies across regions and city types.

## 1. Introduction

Cities are central to global climate change mitigation because they concentrate people, economic activity, infrastructure, and energy demand (Seto et al 2014). Urban areas account for roughly 70% 60

of global final energy use and a similar share of energy-related CO₂ emissions, making them critical sites for mitigation action (Lwasa et al 2022). At the same time, cities offer substantial mitigation opportunities across buildings, transport, energy supply (Creutzig et al 2016), and urban form (Creutzig et al 2015). Many of these actions are cost-effective and deliver significant co-benefits such as improved air quality, health, and accessibility (Becvarik et al 2024, Castillo et al 2021, Creutzig et 65

al 2025).

Despite their central role, the evolution of the urban share in global emissions across sectors and city types remains poorly quantified, limiting the ability to align subnational action with national and global climate targets. Scenarios from integrated assessment models (IAMs) have long served as primary tools for exploring emissions futures (Weyant 2017) providing crucial inputs for climate 70

policymaking (UNFCCC 2023, IPCC 2022), financial risk assessment (NGFS 2024, Bertram et al 2021), and Earth system modeling (O’Neill et al 2016, Gidden et al 2019, van Vuuren et al 2025).

However, IAMs have limited geographical resolution and typically represent 12–32 aggregated world regions, lacking the spatial granularity required to capture subnational heterogeneity, including differences between urban and rural energy use and emission patterns. Very few studies use 75

variants of IAMs to analyze city-level emissions directly. Weber et al. (2024) and Waite et al. (2024) implemented the cities of Kuala Lumpur and Bangkok, respectively, as explicit regions in the Global Change Analysis Model (GCAM) to analyze climate change mitigation strategies for these cities. Using an energy system model, Jacobson et al. (2018) derived transformation pathways for US cities. Other studies used IAMs to estimate urban and rural emissions from the transport and residential 80

energy use in selected countries (Yin et al 2015, Krey et al 2012, Daioglou et al 2012). Still others use IAM-derived scenarios to benchmark subnational mitigation efforts against current national policies or to evaluate their aggregate global impact (Kuramochi et al 2020, Hsu et al under review).


<!-- Page 3 -->


3

However, these approaches do not provide a comprehensive, sector-resolved assessment of the aggregate urban contribution to global emissions across a wide range of mitigation scenarios. 85

Addressing this gap requires downscaling global emissions pathways to the urban scale in a manner that preserves sectoral dynamics and scenario consistency. Downscaling IAM scenarios is an established practice (van Vuuren et al 2010, Grübler et al 2007).  Gurney et al. (2022) combine historical urban per-capita consumption-based CO₂ emissions (Moran et al 2018) with projections from the Shared-Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) to derive urban emission scenarios under 90

alternative socioeconomic developments and global mitigation goals, but do not resolve emissions across sectors or capture sector-specific decarbonization dynamics.

Here, we develop a spatially explicit downscaling framework that links global emissions pathways from the ScenarioMIP–CMIP7 ensemble (van Vuuren et al 2025) with gridded socioeconomic projections and urban settlement patterns. This approach enables the derivation of sector-resolved 95

GHG emission pathways for urban areas, differentiated by world regions and city types. We address three questions: (i) How does the urban contribution to global GHG emissions evolve across sectors under different climate policy scenarios? (ii) How do mitigation potentials vary across regions and city types? (iii) What role do cities play in achieving deep emission reductions consistent with the goals of the Paris Agreement? 100

Our results provide a systematic and sector-resolved perspective on the role of urban areas in global mitigation pathways, offering insights to inform city-level climate strategies, support the alignment of subnational action with national and global targets, and contribute to upcoming assessments such as the IPCC Special Report on Cities and Climate Change.

## 2. Methods

2.1 Global emission scenarios

In ScenarioMIP-CMIP7, seven IAM systems – AIM 3.0 (Hasegawa et al 2017, Fujimori et al 2024), COFFEE 1.6  (Zanon-Zotin et al 2025), GCAM 8s (Calvin et al 2019), IMAGE 3.4 (Stehfest et al 2014) , MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM-GAINS 2.1-M-R12 (Fricko et al 2017, Krey et al 2020, Kishimoto et al 2025), 110

REMIND-MAgPIE 3.5-4.11 (Baumstark et al 2021, Dietrich et al 2019), and WITCH 6.0 (Emmerling et al 2016)  – are used to derive a wide range of plausible emissions futures under different levels of climate policy ambition and alternative assumptions about socio-economic development, energy use, and land use. Socioeconomic development is prescribed based on the narratives and quantitative drivers of the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) (O’Neill et al 2014). 115

Van Vuuren et al. (2025) describe the scenario narratives for the seven illustrative emission and land use futures, ranging from a High emission scenario exploring the upper end of plausible future emissions, to a Very Low emission scenario limiting the overshoot of 1.5°C and returning to below 1.5°C by the end of the century. In view of current country-level backlashes against climate policies and increasing interest in scenarios that study temperature overshoot (Tavoni et al 2026), the 120

scenario set includes several pathways featuring delayed climate action.


<!-- Page 4 -->


4

The High emission scenario is characterized by a global rollback and eventual collapse of climate policies, the breakdown of international cooperation, and nations increasingly prioritizing economic and security interests over mitigation efforts. The High-to-Low emission scenario follows a similar emissions pathway over the first half of the century, albeit driven by a different narrative based on 125

high growth and rapid technological change. After 2060 it assumes a surge in climate policy ambition aimed at drastically cutting emissions and upscaling carbon dioxide removal. The Medium emission scenario assumes the continuation of existing policies and techno-economic trends. Domestic policy targets such as NDCs and net-zero pledges are not included in this scenario unless a corresponding legislation is in place. The Medium-to-Low emission scenario initially assumes current domestic 130

policies and trends as in the M scenario, but moderately increases climate policy ambition after 2040 to reach net-zero CO₂ globally around the end of the century. The Low emission scenario is consistent with holding warming likely below 2°C, reflecting the NDCs for 2030 and achieving global GHG neutrality by 2100. The Low-to-Negative emission scenario assumes a continuation of current policies and trends until 2035. Strong climate policies thereafter trigger deep emission reductions to 135

rapidly achieve net-zero GHG emissions, relying on large-scale carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies in the second half of the century to limit the duration of the overshoot of 1.5°C. The Very Low emission scenario combines the most ambitious and rapid emission reductions with broad sustainability transformations across all sectors. Its goal is to achieve the lowest plausible peak warming through rapid decarbonization of the electricity supply, deep electrification of energy 140

demand sectors, and behavioral shifts in transportation, consumption, and diets while limiting reliance on large-scale CDR options.

For each of the seven scenario narratives, one scenario quantification by a specific IAM model was selected as a marker scenario (Table 1). In this study, we focus on the seven selected marker scenarios for analyzing urban emission futures. 145

2.2 Downscaling of emission scenarios to urban scale

The method for estimating the urban contribution to future global GHG emissions comprises multiple steps (described in detail in Suppl. Mat. S1): (i) downscaling from native IAM regions to country level and harmonization with historical emissions inventories using a well-established method (Gidden et al 2018); (ii) downscaling from country level to grid level with 0.1°×0.1° grid while 155

accounting for dynamic changes in the subnational distribution of GDP and population; (iii) calculation of urban emissions on national and regional levels based on gridded projections of urban population; and (iv) calculation of urban emissions by city type using the typology introduced by Montfort et al. (2026). These steps are calculated separately for each sector and emission species.

Step (ii) is the central element of this methodology. It downscales aggregate country-level emissions 160

for each sector according to the base year spatial pattern of sector emissions (Hoesly et al 2025) adjusted for projected changes in the spatial pattern of socio-economic drivers: gridded  population (Bondarenko et al 2025a, 2025b) for buildings, transport and waste, and gridded GDP (Paprotny 2025) for energy supply and industry. Resulting gridded emissions are shown in Figure 3a and Supplementary Figures S6-S9. 165

In step (iii), following the degree of urbanization (DEGRUBA) approach (Dijkstra et al 2021) we allocate emissions from each grid cell to (1) cities, (2) towns and suburbs (peri-urban zones), and (3) rural areas in proportion to the population share of each category. Throughout this manuscript, urban emissions refer to the aggregate of emissions from cities plus towns and suburbs. We focus on the energy supply, industry, transport, buildings and waste sectors, for which human settlements are 170

dominant contributors. The analysis considers gross fossil GHG emissions from these sectors, excluding AFOLU and international bunkers.. Wherever reported carbon dioxide removal (CDR)refers to economy-wide deployment including non-urban contributions, since the downscaling method does not allow to distinguish urban from non-urban CDR. In these cases, only permanent CDR is considered, excluding land sinks. 175

The grid-based approach used here differs from approaches that calculate urban emissions within administrative boundaries (Yu et al 2026), although the global urban share in territorial emissions are broadly comparable (Yu et al 2026). Importantly, the territorial emissions analyzed here do not account for emissions related to goods and services consumed in cities but produced outside of cities. This approach differs from consumption-based emissions accounting which uses input-output 180

methods downscaled to urban areas (Moran et al 2018, Gurney et al 2022).

## 3. Results

3.1 Wide range of urban GHG emission futures

Urban emissions futures span a wide range across scenarios (Figure 1). In the Medium scenario, consistent with a continuation of current policies, aggregate urban GHG emissions from the energy 185

supply, industry, transport, buildings and waste sectors are projected to decline from 29 GtCO₂e in 2025 to 25 GtCO₂e in 2050, stabilizing thereafter. In the High and High-to-Low scenarios, assuming a rollback of climate policies, urban emissions increase to 32-37 GtCO₂e by 2050. Very Low, characterized by high climate policy ambition and sustainability-oriented development, implies a


<!-- Page 7 -->


7

reduction of gross GHG emissions from urban areas to 3.9 GtCO₂e in 2050, corresponding to a 190

reduction of 21 GtCO₂e compared to Medium.

The development of urban emissions largely reflects the evolution of global GHG emissions in the respective scenarios. We find that urban areas account for 66% of global GHG emissions from the considered sectors in 2025, broadly consistent with studies based on historic inventories (Crippa et al 2021, Yu et al 2026). In Medium, the urban share in global emissions increases gradually to 77% by 195

2100. The urban share in global emissions remains below the urban share in global population. Global average per capita GHG emissions in urban areas in 2025 are 4.6 tCO₂e/cap, around 20% lower than the global average, and range between 5.0 tCO₂e/cap in High-to-Low and 0.5 tCO₂e/cap in Very Low in 2050 (Figure 2).

3.2 Emission trends and mitigation potentials across sectors 200

Urban areas account for around 67% of GHG emissions from energy supply and 75% of those from industry in 2025. These sectors also hold the largest potential for emissions reductions. While emissions from urban energy installations only decline slightly in Medium, Very Low exhibits a 92% reduction in urban energy supply emissions. Urban industry emissions decline by 82% by 2050 relative to 2025 in Very Low. Residual GHG emissions in deep mitigation scenarios are typically 205

dominated by residual fossil fuel use for bulk material production, such as chemicals, steel and cement (Luderer et al 2022, Zanon-Zotin et al 2025).

Urban areas also dominate direct emissions from the buildings sector, accounting for more than 60% of the sector total; these emissions arise mainly from space and water heating as well as cooking. Importantly, the buildings sector also causes substantial indirect emissions associcated with 210

electricity (e.g., for air conditioning or appliances), district heating and construction materials (Cabeza et al 2022). Under territorial accounting, these emissions are represented in the energy supply and industry sectors. In absolute terms, direct buildings emissions are projected to decrease from around 2.3 GtCO₂e in 2025 to around 1.5 GtCO₂e in 2050 in Medium, and to 0.16 GtCO₂e in Very Low – indicating a substantial mitigation potential from energy-efficiency improvements and 215

the electrification of heating and cooking.

Transport demand includes both short-distance trips that are predominantly urban and linked to population density, and long-distance travel and freight that is also strongly correlated to economic activity (Creutzig et al 2022b, Schäfer et al 2009). Energy use and emissions from transport are therefore more spatially distributed, and urban areas only account for around half of the territorial 220

emissions of this sector (excluding bunkers, i.e. international aviation and shipping). Under a continuation of current climate policy ambition (Medium), urban transport emissions are projected to decrease gradually, as the increasing electrification of road transport offsets the increasing demand, in particular in developing and emerging economies. Even in the High and High-to-Low scenarios with weak climate policies, urban GHG emissions from transport stabilize. By contrast, 225

Very Low shows a near-complete elimination of GHG emissions from transport by 2070, corresponding to emission reductions of 2.0 GtCO₂e/yr compared to Medium.

The treatment of municipal solid waste and wastewater generates GHG emissions – predominantly methane and nitrous oxide  almost 80% of which occur within urban areas. Urban waste emissions

amount to around 1.6 GtCO₂e in 2025, corresponding to around 5% of total urban GHG emissions. 230

Mitigation options include waste reduction and improved waste treatment (Oo et al 2024). In Very Low, GHG emissions from waste remain at around 1.1 GtCO₂e through 2070, making this sector an important source of long-term residual GHG emissions under high climate policy ambition.

Even under the high policy ambition in Very Low residual gross GHG emissions from the considered sectors remain at 2.8 GtCO2e (incl. non-urban) and 2.3 GtCO2e (urban areas) in 2070. CDR 235

3.3 Urban emissions across different world regions

In terms of world regions, urban GHG emissions are dominated by East Asia (including China) South Asia (including India) and other Asian countries, which combine for 60% of the global total in 2025 (Figure 3a,b). This dominance reflects these regions’ large shares of global population, high levels of urbanization, and above world-average per-capita GHG emissions in China. African urbanized areas 255

account for only 1.3 GtCO₂e in 2025 due to relatively low urbanization and per-capita GHG emissions well below the global average. Due to growing population, increasing urbanization, and increasing per-capita emissions, Africa’s urban GHG emissions are projected to triple by 2070 under Medium, accounting for 18% of the global total at that point, and 23% under Very Low. OECD countries of Europe, North America and the Pacific combine for one fifth of global urban emissions in 2025. Their 260

urban emissions decline both in absolute and relative terms in Medium. Per-capita urban GHG emissions in 2025 vary widely across world regions, ranging from 1.3 tCO₂e/cap in Africa, to around 2.2-3.7 tCO₂e/cap in South Asia, Latin America, and other Asia, 4.6 tCO₂e/cap in Europe, 7.7 tCO₂e/cap in North America and Pacific OECD, 9.0 tCO₂e/cap in East Asia; 265

and 7.9-9.4 tCO₂e/cap in the fossil-intensive countries of the Middle East and non-EU reforming economies of the former Soviet Union (Figure 3c). Under a continuation of current policy ambition (Medium), per-capita emissions decrease moderately in high-income countries, China and, to a lesser extent, in fossil-intensive countries, while they increase slightly in Africa, Latin America and India. Despite some convergence, regional disparities in per-capita emissions largely persist in 270

Medium. In Very Low, by contrast, GHG emissions decrease in all world regions, and per-capita gross GHG emissions converge to 0.3-1.3 tCO₂e by 2050. 3.4 Urban emissions vary widely across city types 290

To interpret variation in urban GHG emissions across diverse urban systems, we draw on the global city typology developed by Montfort et al. (2026). The typology groups cities with shared characteristics relevant to climate action, thus enabling comparisons among cities facing similar climate-related challenges. It captures the spectrum of urban development (population and population growth, share of population above age 65, population density and its change), 295

socioeconomic development (GDP,GDP growth, and an index of critical infrastructures), and biophysical conditions affecting energy demand (such as heating or cooling requirements). Drawing on existing IPCC nomenclature (Lwasa et al, 2022), we refer to the four types as emerging, rapidly growing, established, and large and megacities. Emerging cities are smaller, lower-income cities with limited infrastructure, low human development, and high cooling needs; rapidly growing cities are 300

economically expanding cities with intermediate infrastructure, low population density, and rapid horizontal growth; established cities encompass wealthier cities with strong infrastructure and limited population and economic growth; and large and megacities are high-density, fast-growing cities with large population and relatively advanced infrastructure but acute cross-sectoral pressures. . Together, these four types cover 69% of urban population, 75% of urban GDP, and 70% of urban GHG emissions 305

in 2025. Within these typologies, established and rapidly growing cities dominate urban GHG emissions in 2025, together accounting for 14 GtCO₂e (Figure 4a). Under Medium, emissions from established and rapidly growing cities decline only gradually, whereas emissions from emerging cities increase over 310

time and eventually exceed those of rapidly growing cities. Hence, without deep mitigation, an increasing share of future urban emissions will come from city types that currently have lower percapita emissions. Under Very Low, by contrast, emissions decline rapidly across all city types, with the largest absolute reductions occurring in established and rapidly growing cities. 315

Per-capita GHG emissions also differ across city types. In 2025, rapidly growing (6.7 tCO₂e/cap) and established cities (6.0 tCO₂e/cap) have the highest per-capita emissions compared with around 2.2– 3.0 tCO₂e/cap in emerging cities and megacities (Figure 4b). The sectoral composition is broadly similar across city types, although rapidly growing cities have relatively larger contributions from energy supply and industry (Figure 4c). Under Medium, per-capita emissions decrease slightly in established, 320

rapidly growing and megacities, but increase modestly in emerging cities. Under Very Low, by contrast, per-capita emissions decline sharply in all city types and converge to below 0.7 tCO₂e/cap by 2050.

4. Discussion and conclusion

Building on a novel sector-detailed downscaling of ScenarioMIP-CMIP7 pathways, our analysis shows that urban areas will account for a dominant and increasing fraction of global GHG emissions, and 335

offer substantial emission reduction potential. Under high climate policy ambition, urban areas can combine for a total of 21 GtCO₂e of GHG emission reductions by 2050 relative to a continuation of current policies and trends, most importantly from transitioning away from fossil fuels for electricity and heat supply, defossilization of industry, and mitigation action in the transportat, buildings and waste sectors. The dominant roles of energy supply and industry indicate that urban mitigation 340

cannot be understood solely through local demand-side interventions in the transport and buildings sectors, but also depends fundamentally on national and global infrastructure transitions. Nonetheless, the demand-side interventions (Creutzig et al., 2022), and especially urban planning (Creutzig et al., 2026), remain important and are areas where municipalities have considerable agency. 345

Urban emissions and emission reduction potentials, both in absolute and in per-capita terms, exhibit pronounced heterogeneity across regions and city types. Asia dominates both current emissions and future mitigation potentials, accounting for around 60% of urban emissions and more than half of the reduction potential. In terms of city types, rapidly growing and established cities hold the largest share in global mitigation potentials. Per-capita emissions levels and mitigation potentials are 350

greatest in fossil-intensive countries of the Middle East, former Soviet Union and China. Urban areas and emerging cities in Africa and parts of Asia are characterized by low per-capita emissions levels. Dedicated climate policies can enable green growth and prevent a replication of emission-intensive structures currently observed in other world regions.

Mitigation requires action across all sectors, world regions and city types. Table 2 illustrates key 355

options for all six sectors, which can facilitate GHG emission reductions (Table 2). Urban planning strategies are particularly relevant for rapidly growing cities and megacities in Asia and Africa (Creutzig et al. 2026). Other strategies, like building retrofit, will be most important for established cities. Although fleet electrification was previously viewed primarily as a strategy for richer OECD countries, energy security concerns and the rapidly declining costs of batteries are accelerating 360

electric vehicle adoption in Chinese cities, increasingly, also in Africa (Gicha et al 2024, Noll et al 2026).

However, residual emissions will remain even under very high mitigation ambition. CDR technologies are thus a crucial component of net-zero strategies. Since CDR technologies tend to be landintensive (Smith et al 2015) most CDR potential lies outside of urban areas. Intra-urban CDR options 365

include urban trees and greening, wood-based construction, and biochar in construction materials; together, these options have been estimated to offer removal potential on the order of ~1 GtCO₂/yr globally (Rodriguez Mendez et al 2024).

Sector Main solutions

Buildings ● heat pumps and low-carbon district heating (Van Heerden et al 2025, Rosenow et al 2025) ● energy efficient buildings (such as energy efficiency standards, passive housing, retrofits) (Ürge-Vorsatz et al 2020) ● compact urban planning (multi-family housing)

Transport ● fleet electrification and charging infrastructure ● compact urban planning and transit-oriented development (Ewing and Cervero 2017, Nachtigall et al 2025) ● cycling and walking infrastructure (Creutzig et al 2022a, Millard-Ball et al 2025, Hinckson et al 2026, Kraus and Koch 2021)

Waste ● waste prevention (Möslinger et al 2023) ● organic waste diversion to avoid methane from landfills (Oo et al 2024) ● landfill methane capture (Oo et al., 2024)

Industry ● steel recycling (Onesmo et al 2024, Wu et al 2025) ● low-carbon cement (e.g.,with biochar) and wood-based construction (Chen et al 2023)

Energy supply ● renewables (rooftop & balcony PV in cities) (Galvin 2026, Zhang et al 2025) ● dynamic pricing and battery storage

CDR ● urban trees (Rodriguez Mendez et al 2024) ● biochar for buildings (Rodriguez Mendez et al 2024) ● wood-based construction (Mishra et al 2022) ● waste incineration with carbon capture and storage (Struthers et al 2022)

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. The downscaling approach assumes that sectoral emission-intensity reductions in urban areas follow national trends, which may not capture differences in transition dynamics between urban and rural areas. The 375

delineation of urban areas based on gridded population and GDP introduces uncertainty regarding the urban classification. Using administrative boundaries rather than only urban grid cells would result in a higher urban share of emissions, because emissions from non-populated areas within municipalities would also be included. In addition, the focus on territorial emissions excludes emissions embodied in traded goods, such as imported food or electricity, and therefore does not 380

capture the full carbon footprint of urban consumption. Finally, uncertainties inherent to IAM scenarios propagate into the urban emission estimates.

Future research could improve understanding of urban emission futures by representing subnational heterogeneity more explicitly, for example by distinguishing urban, rural, and interurban travel in assessments of mobility transitions and by capturing differences in building stocks and energy 385

demand between urban and rural areas. Accounting for the effects of urban planning on energy demand and related greenhouse gas emissions in scenario modeling would further improve the representation of mitigation options specific to cities. Machine learning could facilitate deeper integration of scenario projections with historical emission inventories and other data sources, such as mobility data, satellite imagery, and climate data, thereby improving the spatial downscaling of 390

future GHG emissions.


<!-- Page 16 -->


16

In conclusion, cities are central to achieving deep emission reductions. Realizing the urban mitigation potential requires rapid transformations in the energy supply, industry, buildings, transportation and waste sectors. Urban planning is a central lever to achieving mitigation across building and transport sectors. At the same time, the uneven distribution of emissions and mitigation potential across 395

regions and city types highlights the importance of differentiated, forward-looking strategies. Integrating spatially explicit urban insights into global scenario analysis provides a critical bridge between global climate targets and subnational climate action.
